title: From the Editor — End of the First Run
summary: Final run-ending editorial page steps outside the fiction to reflect on how Rex Fleet grew during production and what kinds of stories the universe can hold next.
settingText: STAR SPLITTER VISIONS EDITORIAL PAGE — DEEP-SPACE PRODUCTION STUDY / CORRIDOR MOTIFS
panelPlan: Design this as a genuine end-of-run editorial page rather than a story splash. Use one large quiet piece of Rex Fleet art—ships disappearing toward a luminous corridor—plus a restrained strip of small production-study motifs such as ship silhouettes, corridor-beacon geometry or location thumbnails.

Keep the artwork subordinate to the letter. Reserve a large, calm, high-contrast text column with magazine-quality spacing and hierarchy. This page should feel like Star Splitter Visions speaking directly to the reader after the story ends.
Do not create fake handwritten notes, fake creator signatures, fake logos, or invented credits. Do not recap Issue 12 visually or tease a specific unannounced Issue 13 plot.
The closing REX FLEET WILL RETURN line should have clear separation and final-page weight.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: When we started building Rex Fleet, the idea was much smaller than the universe it eventually demanded.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The starting point was the corridors: if civilization depends on a network of routes through dangerous space, somebody has to maintain them, defend them, map them and decide who gets to use them. From there came the Fleet, the Verge and the Shards—not simply as opposing factions, but as people with very different relationships to the same roads.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: That gave us the world. The characters changed the book.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Tess, Abby, Naomi, Venn, Jex, Billie and the rest gradually stopped feeling like pieces positioned around a political conflict and started pulling the story in their own directions. Some relationships became more important than we expected. Characters who seemed destined for one role refused to stay there. A story that began with fleets and borders increasingly became about what people do when the institution they belong to no longer gives them an adequate answer.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The Rift changed too. Early on, it was primarily the environment through which these people traveled. By the time we reached the Calm Corridor and the Mirror Star, it had become something much stranger. We still know more about what the Rift can do than the characters do—but not nearly enough to make it comfortable.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Making these twelve issues also taught us what Rex Fleet itself wants to be. It can hold battleships and refugee skiffs, political arguments and engineering problems, strange physics, marketplaces, old grudges, bad jokes and people trying to get dinner through a checkpoint. The enormous things work better when the ordinary things remain visible underneath them.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: That is the part we want to keep exploring.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: This issue closes the first major Rex Fleet story, but it does not close the universe. There are ships we have barely visited, regions we have only named, histories that have only been hinted at, and parts of the Lattice that nobody in this book has seen.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Most importantly, there are still stories we want to tell with these people.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Thank you for reading all the way to the end of the first run—and for giving us the chance to find out what Rex Fleet could become.
